surveyDefinition.title: Running Shoes — consumer survey (U.K.)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on running frequency, purchase drivers, price sensitivity, and sustainability orientation.

segments.name: Performance-Focused Runners
segments.description: High-frequency runners (3+ times per week) who train for races or personal bests. They prioritize cushioning, responsiveness, and durability, and are willing to pay premium prices for shoes that enhance performance and prevent injury. They replace shoes every 300-500 miles and are highly engaged with technical features.

segments.name: Value-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Run or walk for fitness and commuting, 1-3 times per week, often on pavement. They are price-sensitive and look for durable, comfortable shoes at a reasonable price. They are less concerned with the latest technology and more with getting a good deal on a reliable shoe.

segments.name: Sustainability-Conscious Buyers
segments.description: Run regularly (2-4 times per week) and actively seek out shoes made from eco-friendly or recycled materials. They are willing to pay a premium for sustainable options, but are skeptical of greenwashing and want proof of environmental credentials. They may sacrifice some performance for sustainability.

segments.name: Occasional Lifestyle Users
segments.description: Run or jog infrequently (less than once a week) or use running shoes primarily for casual wear, walking, or gym. They value comfort, style, and versatility over performance. They are less loyal to specific brands and more influenced by price and aesthetics. They may not identify as 'runners'.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Running Shoes buyers in U.K.. It asks how people use Running Shoes, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in U.K. who buy or use Running Shoes for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who have bought running shoes in the past 12 months; Individuals who run or exercise regularly (at least once a week); Individuals who are the primary decision-maker for their own shoe purchase. Excluded: Professional athletes whose shoes are provided by sponsors; Businesses purchasing shoes for employees or resale; Children under 18 (unless purchasing for themselves, but typically parent decides).
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy running shoes for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide which pair to purchase based on fit, style, and performance. While some businesses may purchase shoes for employees (e.g., athletic teams), the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
respondentBehaviours: Engages in running or jogging at least occasionally
Purchases athletic footwear for fitness, sport, or casual wear
Researches brands, reviews, and features before buying
May be brand loyal or open to switching based on price/performance
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's running frequency and context, which immediately separates the heavy, performance-driven runners from the occasional lifestyle users. It then moves into their shoe ownership and replacement cycle, setting up the purchase journey. The buying behavior section traces the path from trigger to research to channel to price, ending with the key decision drivers. The preferences section digs into fit, performance, sustainability, and trade-offs, revealing what each segment truly values. Finally, the satisfaction section measures current satisfaction…

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Running Shoes in U.K. — who Individuals who have bought running shoes in the past 12 months; Individuals who run or exercise regularly (at least once a week); Individuals who are the primary decision-maker for their own shoe purchase. The survey targets the end consumer who buys and uses running shoes for personal fitness and lifestyle. This audience represents the primary market for running shoes globally.

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on running frequency, purchase drivers, price sensitivity, and sustainability orientation.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Combination of usage/behavioural and jobs-to-be-done: the primary axis is the intensity and purpose of running (from daily performance training to occasional casual wear), which drives distinct needs for fit, durability, and price tolerance. This separates buyers more meaningfully than price sensiti

segments.name: Performance-Focused Runners
segments.description: High-frequency runners (3+ times per week) who train for races or personal bests. They prioritize cushioning, responsiveness, and durability, and are willing to pay premium prices for shoes that enhance performance and prevent injury. They replace shoes every 300-500 miles and are highly engaged with technical features.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report the highest weekly running frequency, the highest spend per pair, and will rate performance attributes (cushioning, responsiveness, durability) as more important than price or style.

segments.name: Value-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Run or walk for fitness and commuting, 1-3 times per week, often on pavement. They are price-sensitive and look for durable, comfortable shoes at a reasonable price. They are less concerned with the latest technology and more with getting a good deal on a reliable shoe.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report moderate frequency, lower spend per pair, and will prioritize price, comfort, and durability over brand or performance features. They will be more likely to buy on sale or from discount retailers.

segments.name: Sustainability-Conscious Buyers
segments.description: Run regularly (2-4 times per week) and actively seek out shoes made from eco-friendly or recycled materials. They are willing to pay a premium for sustainable options, but are skeptical of greenwashing and want proof of environmental credentials. They may sacrifice some performance for sustainability.
segments.hypothesis: This group will rate sustainable materials and brand transparency as top purchase drivers, and will be willing to pay more for shoes with credible eco-credentials. They will be more likely to research a brand's environmental practices before buying.

segments.name: Occasional Lifestyle Users
segments.description: Run or jog infrequently (less than once a week) or use running shoes primarily for casual wear, walking, or gym. They value comfort, style, and versatility over performance. They are less loyal to specific brands and more influenced by price and aesthetics. They may not identify as 'runners'.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report the lowest running frequency, lower spend, and will prioritize style, comfort, and price over performance features. They will be more likely to buy shoes that can be worn for multiple occasions.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question 'In a typical week, how many times do you go running or jogging?' (cp2) is the most direct behavioural self-report of running frequency, which is the primary discriminator between segments, so it should settle any tie.
notes: Occasional lifestyle users are primarily identified by low frequency (cp2) and non-performance motivations (cp4), plus style/comfort preferences (bb7, pe4) and low information seeking (bb3).
Sustainability-conscious buyers are identified by eco-material importance (pe5, bb7), verification behavior (pe6), and willingness to pay for sustainability (pe7, sf4).
Performance-focused runners are identified by high frequency, race motivation, mileage-based replacement, premium price, and technical feature priorities.
Value-driven commuters are identified by moderate frequency, commuting motivation, price sensitivity, and deal-seeking behavior.
4 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's running frequency and context, which immediately separates the heavy, performance-driven runners from the occasional lifestyle users. It then moves into their shoe ownership and replacement cycle, setting up the purchase journey. The buying behavior section traces the path from trigger to research to channel to price, ending with the key decision drivers. The preferences section digs into fit, performance, sustainability, and trade-offs, revealing what each segment truly values. Finally, the satisfaction section measures current satisfaction…
storyline_notes: Replaced the generic 'category relationship' beat with 'running frequency' as the opening beat, because frequency is the primary segmentation axis and the safest, most concrete question to ask first.
Added a 'replacement cycle' beat in the consumer profile section, which is critical for running shoes as a durable but consumable product, and directly relates to the heavy-user segment's economics.
In the buying behavior section, placed 'price paid' before 'decision drivers' to build up to the most sensitive question, and to allow the decision drivers to be interpreted in light of actual spend.
In preferences, added a dedicated 'fit and sizing confidence' beat, as fit is a top purchase driver and a common pain point in footwear.
Added 'sustainability credentials' as a distinct beat, reflecting the high environmental awareness in the European market and the need to separate the sustainability-conscious segment from others.
In the satisfaction section, included 'problems and friction' to capture injury and comfort issues, which are key differentiators between segments and a major driver of switching.
metadata.classification_reason: Everyday consumers buy running shoes for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide which pair to purchase based on fit, style, and performance. While some businesses may purchase shoes for employees (e.g., athletic teams), the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
